CODE OF PRACTICE FOR LINING OF VESSELSAND EQUIPMENT FOR CHEMICAL PROCESSES
PART X BRICK AND TILE

0. FOREWORD
Indian Institution on 31 neering Sectional neering Division

0.1 This

Standard (Part X) was adopted by the Indian Standards July 1974, after the draft finalized by the Chemical EngiCommittee had been approved by the Mechanical EngiCouncil.

0.2 This standard is being issued in many parts; the brick and tile lining of vessels and equipment is covered in this part, the other types of lining are covered in the remaining parts of thii standard. 0.3 This part gives guidance to manufacturers and users of brick and tile lined vessels and associated plant and equipment including exhaust-dusts, the various types of lining available and on the selection, design, application, testing, inspection and repair, together with recommendations on the design of the items to be lined. Recommendations f&r the lining of associated surfaces in chemical plant where spillage is experienced are included. 0.4 It is desirable that early consultation and exchange of information should be arranged between all parties concerned with the design, use, manufacture, erection and starting up of the vessels and equipment to be lined. Adequate and accurate scale drawings should be available to all parties concerned. 0.4.1 The lining contractor should approve the suitability of those details of design that affect the efficiency of the Gnished lining. Appendii A gives the details of information to be exchanged at thatstage. 05 In the preparation of this standard, assistance has been derived from BS CP 3003 : Part lo-1970 `Lining of vessels and equipment for chemical processes-Part 10 Brick and tile', issued by the British Standards Institution. 0.6 For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test, shall be rounded off in accordance with TS : 2-1960*. + Rules for roundingoff numericalvalues (tied). 3

L

Is : 4682 (Part X) - 1974 The number of significant places retained in the rounded off value should be
the same as that of the specified value in this standard.

1. SCOPE
1.1 This standard (Part X) lays down the recommendations on the design of vessels for brick and tile lining, methods of application of lining, inspection and testing. i2. MATERIALS

261 Types of Bricks 2.1.1 In this part of Code the term `brick' includes tiles as well as bricks of special shapes. 2.1.2. Basically the lining of chemical vessels fall into the groups given in 2.1.2.1 to 2.1.2.7. 2.1.2.1 Red and blue acid resisting bricks (see IS : 4860-1968*) -Most engineering quality bricks are resistant to acids, alkalis and organic chemicals, with the exception of hydrofluoric acid and concentrated caustic alkalis, especially at elevated temperatures. However, for very dilute (1 percent) hydrofluoric acid conditions a reasonable life may be expected from the blue type of acid resisting brick. Attention is drawn to the fact that commercial phosphoric acid contains traces of hydrofluoric acid. 2.1.2.2 Fireclay or similar type bricks -These types of bricks might be used where ~a combination of elevated temperatures and/or corrosive and erosive conditions are encountered. These materials also have certain thermal shock resistance. 2.1.2.3 Highly vitrified linings, like industrial porcelain, chemical stoneware, fusion-cast basalt, glass and fused silica units. 2.1.2.4 Carbon, including grades of bricks impregnated with resins to reduce their porosity and to meet the particular corrosive conditions. These materials are particularly useful for contact with hydrofluoric acid and have good resistance to thermal shock. 2.13.5 Silicon carbide -These materials consist of bonded silicon carbide; they have excellent acid resistance with particular resistance to abrasion and erosion. In addition they have high thermal conductivity and are used where heat transfer or thermal shock resistance are important. 2.1.2.6 Special ceramic materials - Sintered alumina and silicon nitride are examples. A wide range of other special ceramic materials is becoming commercially available for use under unusual `conditions, for example, thermal shock resistance under corrosive conditions. 2.1.2.7 Heat insuhting materials - The most generally used insulating materials for this purpose are fired diatomite bricks. Such materials are

used where it is necessary to protect an outer casing from high temperature, like in duct lining conveying hot corrosive gases. 2.1.3 Bricks used for the lining of vessels should be accurately shaped as well as of uniform dimension to enable them to be laid with the thinnest possible joints; with bricks manufactured according to-IS : 4860-1968* it should be possible to achieve joints of the order of 3 mm. 2.1.3.1 The properties tractor should be apparent sions, freedom from visual Some methods oftesting are 2.2 Corrosion-Resistant specified, agreed between user and lining conporosity, acid solubility, .uniformity of dimendefects like cracks, internal laminations, etc. described in 1% 2839-1964t. Mortars

2.2.1 Attention is drawn to the fact that many corrosion-resistant mortars cannot be applied directly to concrete and metals without the use of an intermediate layer or primer. 2.2.1.1 Corrosi,on-resistant mortars are generally slow to set and harden under cold and cool temperature conditions and it is best to work at temperatures in the range 25�C to 30�C. 2.2.1.2 Bricks and lining tiles should be clean and dry; the latter condition can usually be obtained by drying and storing under warm conditions. This also helps to maintain warm working conditions. 2.2.1.3 Vessels and tools used for mixing mortars on site should be clean. Aiternatively, use may be made of loose disposable polythene lining in vessels used for mixing. Where proprietary mortars are used, th.e manufacturer's instructions should be adhered to. 2.2.1.4 Corrosion-resistant mortars fall into several distinct categories. It will be seen that a wide variety ofmortars is now available. 2.2.2
Hydra& Cement Mortars 2.2.2.1 Hydraulic cement mortars consist of mixtures of suitable inert fine aggregates (clean sharp sand) with a hydraulic binder, such as Portland, high alumina or supersulphated cement. While such mortars may have a useful resistance to many aggressive conditions, they are not comparable In cases of with special mortars described in X2.3,2.2.4, 2.2.5 and 2.2.6. doubt, cement manufacturers should be consulted before the cement is used. 2.2.2.2 Portland cement mortars as a general guide may be taken to contain calcium silicate gel, and to resist any agent which does not attack this material. Thus their resistance to alkaline media and to non-polar organic materials is good, but it is generally considered that they should . not be used in conditions more acid thanflH 6. 2.2.2.3 High-alumina cement mortars are in many respects complementary to Portland cement mortars. In place of the calcium silicate they

temperatures. If more dilute acids are used the water resistance is reduced. It is also possible to increase the resistance of silicate mortars to hot water The appropriate heat and even dilute alkalis by suitable heat treatment. treatment will vary with circumstance but a typical heat treatment will be heating for several hours at l2O"C. . 2.2.3.1 Conventional silicate mortars are inherently permeabIe. Those using silicofluoride type hardening agents are prone to loss of adheBy the use of halogen sion between brick and mortar under acid conditions. free hardening agents, that is, some esters and amines, mortars are available with reduced permeability and greater retention of adhesion under acid conditions. Silicate mortars can be used at higher temperatures than other corrosion resistant mortars. 2.2.4 Rubber Latm Mortars - Rubber latex mortars comprise a suitably stabilized concentrated natural rubber latex and a powder based on a mixture of an hydraulic cement, usually high-alumina cement, with inert fillers and sands. They set and harden by a combination of coagulation of the rubber latex and hydration of the cement. Rubber latex mortars are resistant to water, dilute acids and alkalis~generally in the PH range of 2 to 12. They are attacked by many organic materials and by oxidizing conditions. Their big advantage over other corrosion resistant mortars is that they can be applied under a wide variety of climatic conditions except frost -and can Where differential movement occurs the be applied to damp surfaces. additional resilience of these mortars may be an advantage. It is also possible to formulate mortars of this type based on synthetic rubber latices but little experience is available to date. 23.5 Sul'iur Bonded Mortars - Sulphur bonded mortars are based on powdered sulphur combined with inert fillers, supplied either in powder form So called `plasticized sulphur cements' also incorpoor cast into blocks, rate small quantities of organic compounds or polymers which increase their resistance to thermal shock. They have to be applied by special techniques in a moben form. The inherent high shrinkage of these mortars can be minimized by adjustment of the fillers. Sulphur bonded mortars should not be used at temperatures in excess of 80�C. 2.2.5.I Sulphur bonded mortars have good resistance to water, inorganic acids up to medium strengths and to mild alkalis, like sodium carboA valuable feature nate. They are attacked by even dilute caustic alkalis. is their resistance to hydrofluoric acid and nitric acid up to about 45 percent concentration. Resin Bonded Mortars 2.2.6.1 General - Resin bonded mortars are based on synthetic resins in syrup form, inert fillers and hardening agents for the resin.. Several types are available based on phenolic, furane, cashewnut shell liquid; polyester and epoxide resins. The chemical resistance of these mortars varies somewhat widely and as they are normally available as proprietary products it is 2.2.6

IS : 4682 (Part X) - 1974 most important that the user discusses his requirements fully with the supplier and also if possible makes tests under working conditions. In general, many types are resistant to acids, alkalis (including caustic They are, therefore, of great value in alkalis) and organic compounds. many processes and conditionshaving alternating acid and alkali conditions. Their chief limitation is to oxidizing conditions, such as nitric and chromic acids. Most resin mortars are rather slow in setting and hardening under cold and cool conditions but with temperatures in the 25 to 30�C range will normallv be set and hard within 24 hours. During this time they should be protected with waterproof sheeting. They should always be applied to clean and dry surfaces as the presence of moisture can prevent complete setting and hardening. Ahthese types of mortar have a potential health hazard and it is essential that appropriate precautions be taken in their use. \ 2.3 Compatibility of Corrosion-Resistant Mortars and Protective Membranes - Generally the majority of corrosion-resistant mortars and protective membranes are compatible and may be placed in direct contact without any significant reaction or damage between the two, but attention is drawn to the following combinations which may require special precautions : 4 Silicate mortar with lead or stainless steel membranes; here it is essential that thesilicate mortar is based on halogen free hardening agents. b) Silicate mortar with glass reinforced polyester laminates used as membranes; here it is essential that the polyester resin used in the laminate has good resistance to caustic alkalis. 4 Phenolic or furane type resin mortars with lead or stainless steel membranes; here it is essential to pre-coat the metal surface with a special primer. 4 Polyester resin mortar with natural or synthetic rubber or plasticized PVC membranes; here there is a possible softening effect of free styrene in the resin mortar on the membranes. This hazard is not very serious as most polyester resin mortars set and harden fairly rapidly. In all the above cases consultation should be made with the mortar supplier and the lining contractor and their specific recommendations obtained and implemented. 3. DESIGN OF VESSELS AND EQUrPMENT 3.1 Steel Vessels 3.1.1 Steel vessels lined with corrosion resistant bricks or tiles are used where corrosive or erosive conditions are severe and where suchvessels are not ruled out by other considerations. They are rarely used as jacketed 8 FOR LINING

c

IS : 4682 (Part X) - 1974
They vessels, because of the poor thermal conductance of the brick lining. may also be unsuitable where sudden changes of temperature are involved or where the chemical conditions may be such that no mortar is suitable as in The the case of concentrated nitric acid ~alternating with caustic alkali. instance in which~ceramic linings are technically unsuitable are rare however, and usually the choice between a brick-lined vessel and one lined with another material or made from another material, is governed by cost, weight and reliability; in many cases there is no reasonable alternative. 3.1.2 In general it is recommended that the vessels to be fitted with a corrosion resistant lining should be of welded construction from carbon The inner steel plates using fusion welded butt-joints wherever possible. weld face should be ground off flush and smooth in order to ensure that the lining can be set tight against the shell as this limits the movement of the lining and thus minimizes the risk of joint cracking because of thermal or other movement. 3.1.3 Wherever possible the shape should be simple and symmetrical, such as cylindrical with ends either flat, conical or dished and with as large a radius as possible in anv corners which occur. Irregular shapes can be lined but will be more difficult and costly. 3.1.4 Vessels should be fabricated and tested in accordance with recognized standards of good design and practice to suit the operating conditicns wiih the thickness of the shell and ends being adequate to meet the loads imposed by the lining and to meet the required strength under operating For guidance on these requirements reference pressures and temperatures. may be made to IS: 2825-1969* and IS: 803-19627. Vessels should be rigid enough to prevent deflection from breaking the brittle jointing material Floors may be fully supported. used in linings. 3.1.5 The drawing of the vessel should give full details of construction and the method of lining should also be shown. 3.2 Concrete Constructions - Concrete constructions can be lined with ceramics successfully but it will be clear that if seepage occurs such construction cannot be repaired as simply as a metal vessel (into which a patch can fairly easily be weldedj. 3.2.1 For this reason the constructions should conform to IS : 3370 (Part I)-1965$, IS : 3370 (Part II)-1965$, IS : 3370 (Part III)-1967: and IS: 3370 (Part IV)-1967:. The hydraulic test should be made before starting to install the lining.

However, where a membrane is installed, no relaxation in the standard of fixing the lining should be permitted. 4. DESIGN AND INSTALLATION OF LININGS

consequences of a failure of a brick lining are often "4.1 General -The serious and high-class workmanship is therefore vitally necessary. The standards required are quite different from ordinary bricklaying standards; careful work is essential using well made bricks of uniform size. Misshapen, undersized, and oversized bricks should be rejected. Every joint should be completely filled with mortar and, by buttering and squeezing to eliminate air bubbles, solid joints not thicker than 3 mm should be produced. When using mortars which flow readily it is sometimes necessary to shore the bricks in position to retain a fair face. When work is continuous, the laying speed should be controlled to avoid squeezing out the jointing of previous courses. 4.1.1 Proportioning and fixing of the mortars requires care to ensure correct workability and setting; where proprietary mortars are used the manufacturer's recommendations should be followed. Account should be taken of any unusual ambient temperature conditions or dampness, and where necessary, weather protection should be provided. To meet these requirements, the use of both specially trained tiers and labourers with careful supervision is necessary. 4.2 Protective Membranes - It is advisable in vessel lining to provide a continuous membrane protection applied directly to the metal, concrete or other surface to be lined. This consists of a continuous sheet, as applied or as formed like lead, rubber, asphalt, sheet plastics material or glass reinforced plastics. The membrane behaves effectively as the primary protection, the inner brick lining acting as a protection for the membrane from excessively high temperature, abrasion or other mechanical damage. Protection of the membrane from heat and corrosion is particularly important in ducting carrying hot gases. Nevertheless, every care should be taken to make the brick lining as perfect as possible. The brick or tile lining should in any case be designed to have inherent structural stability. The joints of a membrane lining should not protrude sufficiently to distort the fair face of the brick lining. 402.1 Whatever the material used the membrane should be held tight against the shell to give firm backing for the brickwork and be carried through branches, over flanges, etc. Trapped air or solvent should be avoided because of the danger of disruptive forces on the brickwork during subsequent heating. 10,

~

IS : 4682 (Part X) - 1974 4.2.1.1 The same procedures as described in other par& of this code for these materials are adopted for membranes behind brickwork except that thinner layers may be acceptable and a lead lining may be of sheet lead and Where applied in the sheet form the need not necessarily be homogenous. `rack welding' of the lead to the shell should be the preferred method to obviate protrusions. 4.3 Choice of Lining Matedal - The choice of the class of lining material and mortar, the design of the individual lining units and of the lining as a whole can only be based on the experience of the user and/or lining contractor having regard to the particular conditions of installation and use. 4.4 Design of Joint between Floor and Wall - The joint between flat floors and walls may be made in one of the following ways : The floor may be laid first right to the shell wall, thus avoiding a continuous vertical joint; b) The wall may be built first and the floor laid to it, the vertical joint thus being visible for inspection; and 4 A cove may be used to provide the junction between 0oor and wall, thus avoiding a joint at the most vulnerable point. If coves of the required dimensions are readily available this method of construction is preferred.

a>

4.5 Lining of Floors and koundations 4.5.1 General - The areas in the vicinity of vessels and other equipment handling corrosive fluids are inevitably subject to accidental leaks or spillage. Steps should therefore be taken to protect foundations, structural members and underground services from damage. 4.5.1.1 The information required by the designer responsible for the work includes knowledge of the permeability of the soil together with analysis of solid and ground water or any Cll material which has been used, where corrosive conditions may exist, and an assessment of the origin of such corrosive conditions : plant layout showing layout of floor mounted equipment, drains and other locations where deliberate or accidental discharge of corrosive materials may occur; the chemical composition of such corrosive material together with temperature and rates or likely quantities of continuous or intermittent discharge; proposed methods of floor cleaning like shove&g, washing with hot or cold water, etc. 4.5.1.2 In view of the importance of protecting foundations and .structural members the objective wherever possible should be to achieve inherent resistance to attack rather than surface protection. However, this is frequently not possible in which case a protective system should be used which provides perfect protection. A small failure can cause serious damage and can be extremely difficult to repair, consequently a practical solution should be found to even the smallest problem in design detail. 4.5.1.3 In some cases, instead of a-protective system designed to last the 11

Is : 4682 (Part

X) - 1974

full life of the plant, the best engineering solution may lie in the choice of a For example, in an area normally uncheap, easily replaced material. contaminated there may be a risk of a major acid spillage. A concrete screed over a suitable membrane could be satisfactory provided the overall design, including the drainage system, were capable of resisting such a spibge. The concrete screed could be sacrificed and replaced without damage to any other part of the system. Where this procedure is followed, discussion with +he equipment designers is necessary to ensure the facility for subsequent replacelment of the screed. 4.52 F'oundati,-nr - High qualit\ concrete should be used for all foundations. It shouid be ensured thatSdeterioration of the concrete does ncrt occur which could cause damage to any protective floor covering and lead to more serious damage. Floors shouid be sloped to connecting drain channels located clear of main columns, services, etc. The floor slope should prefcrabiy be -I in 40 but should not be less than 1 in Ml under any circumstances. Surrounding kerbs should be high enough to retain any quantities of spillage that are reasonably foreseeable. 4.5.2.1 Drainage of aoors should be by open channels wherever possible to facilitate cleating; piped drains under such fioors being inaccessible shouid be kept to a minimum. 4.5.2.2 Where surface protectionis provided all concrete pits and drain channels below ground should be safeguarded against the effects of ground water pressure; this should be done by tanking or other effective means however shallow the depth. 4.5.2.3 The stabihtv of the concrete base slab is vital to the success of the protective floor surfacing and in cases of doubtful ground stabilitv piling should not be considered as an unreasonable expense. Where spihage is possible down structural columns or vessel supports, such columns or supports shouid be provided with welded skirts to protect the base-plate or foundation plinths. 4.5.3 ProfectZo Membrane - As with vessel linings, the membrane interlayer behind brick or tile sui?accs (usually polythene, polyisobutylene or plasticized. PI'Cj is to be regarded as the primary protection and the design to be made according!y; it should not be treated as a second line of defence. Provision should be made to ensure freedom of relative movement between the brickwork and the sub&or, thus when pal yisobutylcne membranes arc used, for example, and stuck dawn to the concrete they should be Covered with a layer of building paper or poiythene film to prevent adhesion 1.o the brickwork. In genera:, ii shouid be noted that such. sticking down is done in order to facilitate construction and is not a primary requirement. Cnnsequently action should not be taken which might be detrimental to the effectiveness ofthe compiete work merely in order to stick down a membrane, Where organic solvents may be present polythene should be used in preference to either polyisohutylene or plasticized PVC. 12

IS : 4682 (Part X) - 1974 4.5.4 : Expansion Joints - Particular care should be taken &I the construction of expansion joints especially where a protective membrane is used The joint should not penetrate this membrane behind brick or tile surfaces. as otherwise the whole function of the membrane in providing a liquid tight seal will be lost. The choice of material for the expansion joint will depend up011 the corrosive conditions to be met with and should be agreed after discussion between the user and the flooring contractor, one of the more suitable being types based on polysulphide synthetic rubbers. The general principles given in 4.5.4.1 and 4.5.4.2 are recommended. 4.5.4.1 Floor-s :CI~&IU~ continuous membranes - Expansion joints should begenera!ly provided at the periphery of all areas and this will be the case adjacent to wails and also around coh~mns and other upstands which project through the normal floor surface. Expansion joints should also be provided to correspond with any expansion joints in the sub-floor or base. In certain cases, because of the arrangements of the tiling or paviors, this may not be possible but the bond should be broken as close to the expansion joint as possible by means of strips of building paper in the tiling. In cases where there is frequent or continuous spillage of hot iiquids the above provisi.ons should be provided and also additional expansion joints should be provided in the floor surface so as to give bays not larger than 12X12 m. 4.5.4.2 FLOWSwith continuous membranes - In general it is, of course, inadvisable to cut through the membrane in order to provide an expansion joint and therefore expansion joints will be confined to the tiling or paving construction. Most of the conventional membranes have some degree of resilience or `give' which will help in itselfto provide some measures of expansion joint effect. Expansion joints in the tile or paving floor should be provided at ali periphery areas and around columns and upstands. These will normally be sited one tile course away from the periphery which may often be in the form of a cove. In these cases the membrane will usually be turned up for a short distance around the upstands to give complete protection in these areas. 4.5.5 B,icks or 73s - Cutting of bricks should be reduced to a minimum not only because this reduces the cost but because the cutting of bricks increases the difficulty of making a good job. 4.5.5.1 Where drain channels are provided the concrete base to the invert sh~dd. first be stepped at intervals so as to make the steps equai :o the thickness of one brick course. After the membrane has been applied the side-walls are then built with little or no cutting required~; sloping screed in suitable corrosion-resistant mortar is laid to form the fall between the steps following which the drain invert is to be laid in plain brickwork. 4.5.5.2 Similarly where kerbs are provided along a sloping floor surface 13

c

IS : 4682 (Part

X) - 1974

it is unnecessary to cut bricks in order merely to produce horizontal joints in the kerb. 4.5.5.3 Where small items of equipment, such as pumps are installed the brick of the tile lining on the floor should be carried continuously beneath the plinth, the latter being formed in brickwork alone or concrete In many cases timber plinths or bearers may be protected by brickwork. preferable. 4.5.5.4 Structural steel columns should be protected by founding the base below floor level and casing the column in concrete 300mm above the .-floor. The protective system used for the floor should be carried up this casing. 4.5.6 Surface Protection- In some situations surface protection may be provided with epoxide resin self-leveliing screed but this has rather limited application and is not suitable for severe corrosive conditions, hot spillage or where cleaning operations, such as shovelling, can causemechanical damage. A floor which will tolerate somewhat more severe conditions is provided by , an epoxide resin screed sealed with a resin-rich surface to reduce porosity. Where epoxide resin coatings are employed the concrete should be clean, The invert and lqwer walls dry and free from laitence and contamination. of drain channels should always be brick lined to withstand drain cleaning operations. 4.5.6.1 Where maintenance work or coating of old concrete is necessary it may be preferable to use an epoxide resin `membrane' rather than a sheet membrane. 4.6 Installation of Lining - Though it is possible to go into great detail about methods of lining in a code of practice of this nature only general principles are indicated. 4.6.1 Before lining is commenced the surfaces to be lined should be thoroughly cleaned and dry; v:here these surfaces are of ferrous metal they should be free from loose scale and rust. For outdoor installations a temporary weather protection, for example, waterproof sheeting, may be necessary. It may be necessary in some cases to prime the surfaces to prevent interaction with the mortar. Clarification of this point should be obtained with the supplier of the mortar. ,4.6.1.1 Where no membrane is used the shell of a vessel or other surface should, after cleaning and if necessary, priming, be skimmed with mortar and the backs of the bricks well buttered to ensure both a continuous layer behind the lining and good contact between bricks and shell thereby minimizing movements which could cause cracking. With a membrane good contact only is necessary and the initial skimming may be omitted. 4.6.2 Close dimensional tolerances -of the bricks or tiles are desirable especiallyfor width and~depth. Closer tolerances on a particular dimension They can can be achieved by sizing the bricks with a sizing machine. 14

L

IS : 4682 (Part X) - 1974 then be sorted into groups which are all within 1 mm for this dimension. Thin joints can be achieved by using bricks in one group for each course, It is likely that it will be possible to buy bricks ready sized, though at some extra cost. In order to preserve close tolerances, cutting and trimming should only be done with a brick saw or grinding wheel, not with ahammer and chisel. 4.6.2.1 Should tongued and grooved tiles be used. attention is drawn to the necessity to preserve this beneficial feature, by making certain that the tongue or groove is not chipped, and that-every joint is filled, particularly Closures should be cut so as to maintain the where closuresare inserted. Various other forms of -interlocking minimum joint thickness specified. tiles are also available. 4.6.2.2 Some vessels can be most economically lined wholly, or nearl? so, using rectangular bricks or tiles of standard sizes which are convenient Other shapes and to handle and are, in general dimensionally accurate. sizes are also used. 4.6.2.3 In some cases it may be impracticable to use standard rectangular shapes, for example, a small diameter vessel is better lined with arch or circle bricks. To avoid unnecessary expense the use of a large number of special shapes, should, if possible, be avoided; it is nearly always possible to use standard shapes, cutting with a brick saw where necessar! unless much cutting is required which may then necessitate purpose-made bricks or tiles. 4.6.3 Bonded brickwork should be used, and in double linings the joints in the two layers should not coincide. In laying the floor the pattern should be such that the minimum of cutting is required at the perimeter (see Fig. 1). 4.6.3.1 Closures are a source of weakness in corrosion-resistant brickwork and various schemes have been devised to minimize the number required depending on the type of the tile, size and shape of vessel, etc. Great care is necessary in fitting them to ensure that the joints are well filled. The most satisfactory method is to use a brick cut diagonally into two wedges which can be fitted easily with well filled, tight joints of the thickness specified. 4.6.3.2 The simple arrangement for lining the walls of vertical tanks is to lay separate courses, with continuous horizontal joints. Joints between If continufloor and wallrequires only one closure per course (see 4.4). .ous horizontal joints are thought undesirable because of the possibility 01 erosion of the mortar the bricks are laid in a diagonal pattern, as shown in Fig. 2. Wooden battens are first wedged in place, and bricklaying carried out as in Fig. 2A. When the cement has hardened, the battens are removed, the bricklaying is continued as in Fig. 2B. The remainder of the wail is then lined as in Fig. 2C and 2D, with one wedge-type closure per course. If the `vessel is too deep for this procedure, say more than 2 m 15

For small branches special lining pieces may be used which are in effect flanged pipes, the flanges being of such shape and thickness that they form part of the vessel lining. Alternatively, a plain stoneware pipe may be cemented into the branch, flush with the lining. For pipes up to 150 mm diameter a special large tile with a hole to fit the pipe may be fitted; for large diameter openings circle or arch bricks should be used. 16

typical arrangements, that in Fig. 4C generally gives the soundest CO~S~~UCtion. Plastics or special metal,linings may be used in branches, in ~which case the lining should be flanged, the flange being adjacent to the flange of . the branch. 4.7 Prestressed
Ceramic Linings

4.7.1 Prestressed ceramic linings are limited to,lining for cylindrically shaped miid steel vessels and similar equipment, but the vessels may have domes or coned ends. 4.7.X.1 By means of the prestressing technique a major limitation of The coefficient of thermal ceramic linings to steel vessels can be overcome. expansion of most ceramic linings is about half that of mild steel. As a result, with the use of liquids at elevated temperatures, there is a tendency for the steel shell or `outer' to expand to a greater degree than the inner ceramic lining, in spite of some temperature drop through the thickness of the lining. There is thus a tendency for the steel shell to move outward from the ceramic lining and subject the latter to tensile stresses. .Cracks can then develop (usually in the joints) or gaps can form behind the lining and allow the liquid in the tank to reach the steel outer shell. 4.7.X.2 Attempts shall be made to minimize this difhculty by increasing the thickness cf the ceramic lining and so increasing the temperature drop through the lining. Whilst this can be of help it does not completely solve the problem in al! cases and the costs are very considerably increased. 4.7.2 Special corrosion resistant mortars are available which have the property of swel!ing slightly under suitable heat treatmentwithout diminishing their adhesion to the ceramic units used for the lining of,.or to the steel outer shell of, the vessel; their use results in a prestressed hnmg. This puts the steel shell in tension whilst the ceramic lining is in compression. 4.7.2.1 Ceramic linings withstand compressive stresses well. The prestressing operation is carried out by filling the lined vessel with a liquid and slowly bringing the temperature and pressure up to a designed excess over the maximum proposed working temperature and pressure. These conditions are held for some hours and then the vessel is allowed to cool down very sIowly to the normal ambient conditions. After this treatment the ceramic lining will remain permanently in compression provided the prestressing temperature and/or pressure is not exceeded. It is~necessary that the prestressing operation is carried out within a few weeks of the installation of the lining as after this period of time the swelling property of the mortar is lost. 4.75 Owing to the calculations that are necessary for the successful installation of a prestressed lining the use of such a lining should only be made after full consultation with the designer. The joints in such a lining may be significantly wider than that recommended in 4.1. 20

_

IS : 4682 (Part X) - 1974 5. SUPERVISION, TESTING, INSPECTION AND REPAIR

5.1 Supervision, Testing and Inspection - It is not easy to apply any test to ceramic linings. The only satisfactory method of ensuring a sound job is to have experienced supervision during erection, to see that the mortar is correctly mixed, that the technique Is correct and that joints are of the correct width and are properly filled. Attention should also be paid to the following: a) Brick cutting should be done by a saw and not by hand, b) Mortars should not be re-tempered once they have started to set, and c) For most mortars the bricks should be completely dry before and after laying until the mortar has hardened. 5.1.1 These and similar points can be watched by an inspector, but once the work is completed there is no easy way testing the structure. 5.1.2 Provision should be made for the work to be accepted or rejected stage by stage before the mortar hardens to such an extent that removal of unsatisfactory work may cause damage. 5.2 Repair - If a failure occurs in a ceramic lining, as shown either by examination of the lining, or more usually by attack on the shel1, it is always tempting to carry out a local repair. This can sometimes be done by forcing in an appropriate mortar or by ~repointing, and this may be successful temporarily. It is often found, however, that unless the fault can be clearly seen the repair is ineffective. Penetration of the shell may occur far away from the origin of the fault, the liquor having flowed between the shell and the lining to accumulate further down. Moreover, the cutting out of the lining may, unless very carefully done, start cracks in the adjacent sound lining. It may be found to be quicker and cheaper in the long run to replace the entire lining at the earliest opportunity, and at the same time to make the shell completely sound by replacing holed or badly thinned areas. However, when patching is necessary, the area to be patched should be cut out using a diamond saw to minimize disturbance. 5.2.1 Most corrosion-resistant mortars will not harden in contact with wet ceramic and any acid present on the surface may cause flash setting. If an attempt is made to repair a lining, great care is, therefore, necessary to ensure that the surrounding surfaces are clean and dry. They can be well washed with water and then dried by a blast of hot air. The mortar should then be applied immediately, preferably using a cement modified to give quick setting. In this way a successful repair may be possible, provided the lining left in place is sound.

Early consultation and exchange of information should take place between the liniig contractor and All parties concerned in the design, manuComplete facture, erection and use of the vessels and equipment to be lined. --and accurate scale drawings should be made available to all parties concemed. The consultation should cover the following : Site conditions, which affect this work, including, location on site and weight of the lined vessel; b) -Safety measures to be taken during lining on site; 4 Construction of equipment to be lined, location of welds, type and finish of joints and internal and external supports, general method of lining with regard to structural stability; Nature and concentration of media for which vessel and equipment is required; Apparent porosity and acid solubility of lining material; Operating temperatures and pressures; Other factors influencing material stress; Presence of abrasives in contents and potential local erosion by fluids; and Internal or external installations and means of access, lifting facilities, etc.
